prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
required_recommendations: Restart rifaximin 550 mg BID and arrange supply (case management / patient assistance program).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 18) — precipitated by rifaximin non-adherence x 10 days (insurance gap) plus diarrhea-associated hypokalemia; low-grade fever requires SBP exclusion.

differential.key_features: Blood/urine cultures and CXR — any infection is an HE precipitant in cirrhosis.
Less suggested by tox; monitor regardless.
CT head excludes given coagulopathy + cirrhosis fall risk.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Medication-access gaps (insurance, copays) are common, often missed precipitants — ask about pill supply directly.
Rifaximin secondary prophylaxis is a 1A indication after a first overt HE episode (AASLD).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Cirrhotics have blunted febrile and leukocyte responses; SBP can present with subtle signs — paracentesis is mandatory.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss SBP without paracentesis because fever is low-grade.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 64-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 18), prior HE episode, and a robust HE prophylaxis regimen, brought by his sister for acute confusion and agitation over the past 3 days. She confirmed he had been out of rifaximin for 10 days due to an insurance authorization issue. Over the prior 5 days he had 4-5 loose stools/day, initially attributed to lactulose. He also has a low-grade fever and had a respiratory illness 2 weeks prior. His ammonia is 142 µmol/L — markedly elevated. EEG shows classic triphasic waves. CT head is normal.
